MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Council Chambers, 111 South First Street
  April 27, 2026
  6:00 p.m.
ROLL CALL: At 6:09 p.m., on Monday, April 27, 2026, the Alhambra City Council met in the Council
Chambers of Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  LEE, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
ABSENT:  MAZA

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, Assistant City Manager Garcia, City Attorney Montes,
Assistant City Clerk Lamb McCarthy, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director of Finance
Lieu, Director of Community Development Ho, Planning Manager McCurley, Director of Public Works
and Utilities Ahlen, Chief of Fire Department Ragusa, Chief of Police Kennedy, Director of Library
Services, LohGuan, Director of Human Resources Ko, Management Analyst Alvarez, Economic
Development Specialist MacCarley

FLAG SALUTE:  Led by Mayor Maloney

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to prioritize
respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples throughout California,
especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with respect and gratitude for the
Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the caretakers of this land. It is through their
examples that we are reminded of our greater responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take
care of each other.

MAZA:  Councilmember Maza entered Council Chambers at 6:11 p.m.

CEREMONIALS

1.  PROCLAMATION: OLDER AMERICANS MONTH – F2M26-3

  The Alhambra City Council ratified the action of Mayor Maloney in proclaiming the month
  of May, 2026 as OLDER AMERICANS MONTH in Alhambra. Mayor Maloney presented
  the Older Americans Month proclamation to Director of Parks & Recreation Michael
  Macias.

2.  COMMENDATIONS: ALHAMBRA HIGH SCHOOL ACADEMIC DECATHLON TEAM –
  F2M25-3

  Mayor Maloney and the Alhambra City Council wished to congratulate and commend the
  Alhambra High School 2026 Academic Decathlon Team. For the third year in a row, the
  Team took first place out of 61 teams in the 44th Annual Los Angeles County Academic
  Decathlon, after an outstanding performance in 10 subject areas including art, economics,
  literature, mathematics, science, music, social science, essay, speech and interview. The
  Team scored a total of 49,044 points and took home a total of 52 Medals. The Team then
  went on to place 6th in the California State Finals earning an additional 17 individual
  medals. The AHS Academic Decathletes are to be commended for their perseverance
  1
4-27-26
   and dedication to scholastic excellence and the City of Alhambra celebrates their
  remarkable accomplishments. Mayor Maloney presented commendations to the AHS
  2026 Academic Decathlon Team members and coach. Head Coach Jose SANCHEZ
  spoke on behalf of the team and discussed their accomplishment. Team Head Captain
  MD Hamza KHAN thanked Council and discussed the team’s performance. The Team
  members were as follows:
  MIYEKO CAPELA
  CARLOS CARRANZA JR.
  YINGHAO "AARON" DU
  MD HAMZA KHAN
  TRISTAN LAU
  MICHAEL NGO
  JOAQUIN SALAS
  WILL SAN
  ALEXANDER TRAN
  Head Coach JOSE SANCHEZ
  Asst. Coach CESAR GONZALEZ

3.  COMMENDATIONS: OUTGOING COMMISSION MEMBERS – F2M26-3, F2M26-29

  The City Council, on behalf of the citizens of Alhambra, wished to recognize the City’s
  outgoing Board and Commission members for their outstanding and dedicated service to
  the City of Alhambra. The Commissioners each thanked Council for their time serving
  Alhambra. Mayor Maloney presented the Certificates of Service to the following:
  ERIC GARCIA
  Planning Commission

  BONITA SHARMA-NGAN
  HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee

  JOYCE AMARO
  Historic Preservation Commission

  CHEN YU WANG
  Youth Commission

PUBLIC COMMENT FOR NON-AGENDIZED ITEMS (TIME LIMITATIONS: 3 MINUTES PER
SPEAKER, 30 MINUTES TOTAL) - F2M26-4

  1) Lewis McCammon spoke regarding Item No. 2 and the success of the 2026 Alhambra
  High School Academic Decathlon team. He also congratulated Mark Keppel High School
  for achieving second place in the Los Angeles Academic Decathlon competition. He went
  on to discuss Item No. 3 and commended the outgoing commissioners for their hard work
  in service to the City.

  2) Natasha (Xiaoling) Wang, representing Qzone Billiards Hall, shared her concerns
  regarding a recent Planning Commission meeting for her business’s Conditional Use
  Permit.

  2
4-27-26
   3) Brent Herrington, representing Dryer Vent Wizard, spoke regarding dryer vent building
  code compliance.

  4) Holly Pendergast, via Zoom, spoke in support of tenant protections including relocation
  assistance for no-fault evictions.

  5) Neha Saxana, via Zoom, spoke in support of tenant protections including relocation
  assistance for no-fault evictions.

PRESENTATIONS

4.  STATE OF THE CITY ADDRESS – F2M26-16

  Mayor Maloney delivered the State of the City Address. The presentation is on file in the
  City Clerk’s office. Mr. Maloney provided insight on the current state of the City and the
  progress that has been made over the past year.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the informational report.

5.  TRAFFIC CALMING GUIDELINES POLICY  UPDATE  AND  REVISIONS
  RECOMMENDATIONS – F2M24-33, M2M26-67

  Deputy Director of Public Works CHAN delivered a staff report and Jenna ROBERTS,
  from Transtech, delivered a presentation, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office. On May
  12, 2025, the City adopted Traffic Calming Guidelines to address neighborhood concerns
  related to motorized traffic and pedestrian safety. The Guidelines established a structured
  and transparent process for evaluating and implementing appropriate traffic calming
  measures on residential streets, with the goal of enhancing neighborhood livability while
  maintaining safe and efficient traffic flow. Since the program began, the City has received
  and addressed eleven traffic calming applications. Additionally, there were nineteen traffic-
  related questions submitted via GoAlhambra, emails, and phone calls. For these requests,
  staff explained the traffic calming process, however, no formal applications were received.
  After one year of implementation, staff identified opportunities to refine the Guidelines and
  presented to the City Council recommended revisions.

  Public Comment:  Lewis McCammon discussed the reduced speed limit on major
  arterial streets, such as East Main Street, and noted that drivers have not changed their
  behavior. He suggested a Level 2 measure, such as painting the street with the new speed
  limit. He went on to discuss U turns on Main St. and improper parking behavior.

  Discussion:  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER stressed the importance of the
  Transportation Commission’s role in reviewing the Traffic Calming Guidelines Policy. Ms.
  ANDRADE-STADLER and Ms. ROBERTS discussed the differences between collector
  streets and arterial streets, noting several homes were located on collector streets. Ms.
  ANDRADE-STADLER stated that the state guidelines need to be updated to reflect
  changes in urban planning.

  Councilmember WANG supported Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s comments regarding the need
  for the involvement of the Transportation Commission. She further discussed ways to
  improve safety on collector streets, such as speed humps, with Ms. ROBERTS. She
  expressed appreciation for ongoing updates.
  3
4-27-26
   Councilmember MAZA supported the progress of the policy and the recommendations
  staff provided.

  Councilmember LEE discussed the lessons learned from the implementation of the plan,
  discussed the residential applications received and further noted comments received from
  local business owners about the area of Chapel Ave and Main St. She suggested the City
  seek input from business owners. Ms. LEE and Ms. CHAN discussed coordination
  between Police Department and Public Works to collect traffic data and identify other
  problem areas. Ms. CHAN provided additional clarification. They also discussed methods
  for staff to engage with the public. Mayor MALONEY and Ms. LEE discussed her
  suggestion to enhance the process to include a mechanism for businesses to report
  issues. City Manager BINNQUIST stated that while the guidelines were specifically for
  residential areas, all applications for arterial streets are also reviewed by staff to determine
  if traffic calming measures were appropriate. Ms. LEE suggested a separate process for
  businesses to submit requests. Mr. MALONEY and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed the ability
  for businesses may email staff directly with their concerns. Ms. CHAN stated that language
  could be added for business owners.

  Mayor MALONEY discussed the background of the policy to address public concerns. He
  spoke in support of hte policy. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER and Ms. CHAN discussed the
  method to conduct studies after implementation of traffic calming methods in two years.
  Ms. ROBERTS provided clarification. Ms. WANG and Ms. CHAN discussed the city’s
  communication with the public after reviewing an area.

  Mayor MALONEY discussed the purpose of the policy, the need to address safety
  concerns for arterial streets as well as residential streets, and supported staff
  recommendations for changes. Mr. MALONEY discussed MUTCD controls versus other
  methods such as bulb outs and traffic circles with Ms. BINNQUIST and Ms. ROBERTS.
  Mr. MALONEY addressed comments regarding pedestrian concerns and discussed the
  “Walk, Bike, Move Alhambra: Bicycle and Pedestrian Plan.”

  Ms. LEE discussed the need to review the efficacy of traffic calming methods available
  and to make Alhambra’s methods coordinate with other cities. She requested annual
  review of the policy and Ms. BINNQUIST provided clarification.

  Mr. MALONEY called for a motion and reiterated that some changes would be under the
  Pedestrian Improvement Plan. He requested an update on both plans in a year’s time.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the proposed Traffic Calming Guidelines
  Policy revisions recommendations as outlined in the April 27, 2026 staff report by the
  Director of Public Works and Utilities.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  LEE
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, LEE, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

6.  PRESENTATION REGARDING THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA’S DRAFT HOTEL MARKET
  AND FEASIBILITY STUDY – F2M26-25

  4
4-27-26
   Economic Development Specialist MACCARLEY delivered a staff report and presentation.
  The City of Alhambra commissioned HVS to conduct a hotel market and feasibility analysis
  to evaluate the City’s ability to attract a new hotel that would serve both residents and
  visitors. HVS inspected the market area and multiple potential sites and analyzed the hotel
  market conditions in Alhambra and the surrounding areas. From a demand perspective,
  HVS found that the most likely profile for new hotel development in Alhambra would be an
  upper-midscale (such as Holiday Inn, Hampton Inn, and Best Western Plus) or upscale
  limited-service hotel (such as DoubleTree, Wyndham, and Hilton Garden Inn), given the
  gap in current supply and the potential market clientele’s ideal price points. Key
  considerations for hotel development included ease of access, proximity to major
  freeways, and adjacency to established commercial corridors. However, from a financial
  perspective, based on HVS analysis of a potential upper-midscale hotel, a new hotel was
  not financially feasible under current assumptions where development costs (land
  acquisition, permitting, and construction) were projected to be higher than hotel revenue.
  Feasibility could be achieved with an incentivized structure, such as reduced land cost or
  other forms of monetary support. The feasibility gap could also be mitigated if
  complementary uses, such as retail or residential, were developed alongside the hotel and
  were able to share infrastructure and development costs. Because current market
  conditions would not make a hotel developer feasible, this effort would be reprioritized
  until market conditions change. Staff would continue to monitor market conditions and re-
  engage with the hotel development community should anything change.

  Discussion:  Councilmember LEE discussed the study with Ms. MACCARLEY.
  She expressed she did not support a hotel in Alhambra and noted the number of AirBnB
  and Short-Term Rentals. She also stated that at the time, residents did not support a hotel
  due to traffic concerns.

  Councilmember MAZA expressed surprise at the study and the lack of support for a hotel.
  He briefly discussed the amenities of a hotel in Downtown Alhambra and supported staff
  continuing to reach out to the hotel industry. Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER echoed
  Mr. Maza’s comments.

  Councilmember WANG also commented on the demand and the benefits of a hotel,
  including the upcoming Olympics in Los Angeles. She suggested a boutique hotel with
  unique architecture. She also suggested staff continue to monitor the market.

  Mayor MALONEY and Ms. MACCARLEY discussed the large hotels in neighboring cities
  and the potential impact on Alhambra. Mr. MALONEY also discussed Short Term Rentals
  and the demand for occupancy in Alhambra, the depletion of available housing stock, and
  potential locations for a boutique hotel in Alhambra. He also briefly discussed a Transit
  Occupancy Tax and continued to support staff continuing to seek out interested parties.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this report.

7.  CONSIDERATION OF A RESOLUTION ADOPTING A POLICY TO IMPLEMENT NEW
  BROWN ACT AMENDMENTS REGARDING MEETING DISRUPTION PROCEDURES
  PURSUANT TO SENATE BILL 707 – F2M26-24, R2M26-9

  City Clerk MYLES delivered a staff report. On October 3, 2025, Governor Newsom signed
  into law Senate Bill 707 (SB 707), which amended the Brown Act with the intent to diversify
  and increase public engagement during local government meetings of legislative bodies,

  5
4-27-26
   such as the City Council. Among the various new requirements under SB 707, all qualified
  legislative bodies must now offer hybrid meetings (through a two-way phone or video
  platform). The City has already provided hybrid meetings via Zoom since 2020. In addition,
  SB 707 would require the City to formally adopt a policy that outlines how to restore any
  hybrid meeting broadcast disruptions that prevent the public from virtually attending and
  participating in a meeting on or before July 1, 2026. Staff prepared a resolution to satisfy
  this new State requirement. The Disruption of Telephonic or Internet Service Policy mirrors
  the meeting disruption guidelines that are already outlined in SB 707, which requires the
  legislative body to take a recess and try to restore service for at least one hour. If service
  cannot be restored within one hour, the legislative body must conduct a roll call vote
  confirming that good faith efforts were made and the public interest in continuing the
  meeting outweighs remote access. (Cal. Gov. Code §54953.4(b)(1).) The proposed
  Resolution outlined the actions that would take place if disruptions were to occur. If
  adopted, the requirements will go into effect immediately. Staff recommended adopting
  the proposed resolution to reflect the recent legislative changes under SB 707.

  Discussion:  Mayor MALONEY and Ms. MYLES discussed the proposed
  process to restore the meeting.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M26-9 entitled: A
  Resolution of the Alhambra City Council adopting a Disruption of Telephonic or Internet
  Service Policy pursuant to Government Code Section 54953.4

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  MAZA, LEE, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 8 – 24): (TIME LIMITATIONS: 5 MINUTES PER SPEAKER
FOR ONE ITEM, 10 MINUTES PER SPEAKER FOR 2+ ITEMS)
All items listed under the Consent Agenda, with the exception of Items No. 8, 22, and 24, were
considered by the City Council to be routine and were enacted by one motion.

8.  LETTER OF CONCERN REGARDING MICROENTERPRISE HOME KITCHEN
  OPERATION (“CLUB COWBOY CHEDDAR”) – F2M26-7, M2M26-62

  On April 13, 2026, the City Council directed staff to prepare a letter of concern to be
  transmitted to Supervisor Hilda Solis and the Los Angeles County Department of Public
  Health regarding a reported Microenterprise Home Kitchen Operation (MEHKO) operating
  under the name “Club Cowboy Cheddar,” located at 3333 Balzac Street. During the City
  Council General Public Comment period on April 13, 2026, several residents from the
  surrounding neighborhood appeared before the Council to express concerns regarding
  the reported operation. The City’s objective was to support safe and livable residential
  neighborhoods. Based on the concerns raised by residents, the reported activity impacted
  quality of life in Alhambra and may not be consistent with applicable MEHKO program
  requirements. Accordingly, the purpose of the letter was to request the Los Angeles
  County Department of Public Health conduct a thorough investigation into the reported
  operation, including verification or denial of permit, compliance with MEHKO
  requirements, and address any other applicable violations.

  6
4-27-26
   Discussion: Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER requested City Manager BINNQUIST
  provide clarification. Ms. BINNQUIST explained the background and provided an update
  regarding a phone call with Supervisor Solis’s office. Ms. BINNQUIST also provided an
  update as to staff’s action and coordination with Los Angeles County offices. Ms.
  ANDRADE-STADLER discussed the concerns of residents.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the letter as outlined in the April 27, 2026
  staff report by the Assistant City Manager and Management Analyst and directed staff to
  send the letter to Supervisor Hilda Solis and the Los Angeles County Department of Public
  Health. (M2M26-62)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

9.  NOTICE INVITING BIDS: CONSTRUCTION OF POPPY PARK – F2M24-57, N2M26-48

  Staff applied for, and was awarded grant funding from the State of California, under the
  2023 Budget Act with assistance from Assemblymember Mike Fong, to construct a pocket
  park, which was in accordance with the City Council’s Strategic Plan objectives for
  expanding green space. The grant agreement with the State was fully executed, and all
  project funds must be disbursed by June 30, 2030. The planned scope of work included:
  construction of Poppy Park; adaptive reuse of beams from the previous Library building to
  a pergola; and installation of irrigation, landscaping, and walking paths.

  Discussion:  None

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized circulating a Notice Inviting Bids to
  prospective contractors for the construction of Poppy Park, located at 2037 South Fremont
  Avenue, with bids due on May 28, 2026; and, direct staff to undertake the steps necessary
  to finalize the Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

10.  AWARD CONTRACT: 2026 USDA SUMMER FOOD SERVICE PROGRAM – F2M26-24,
  N2M26-17, C2M26-23, M2M26-63

  On February 9, 2026, the City Council approved the distribution of a Notice Inviting Bids
  for the 2026 Summer Food Service Program. Staff included the following food vendors in
  the bidding process: Food Service Outreach, Inc., San Gabriel Unified School District,
  Preferred Meals, School Nutrition Plus, Inc., Unity Meals, and Everytable. On Thursday,
  April 16, 2026, the City Clerk received two bids in the amounts of $97,020.00 and
  $99,691.00. The bid received by School Nutrition Plus, Inc. was the lowest responsive bid.

  Discussion:  None.

  7
4-27-26
   Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to the final language
  approved by the City Manager and City Attorney, to School Nutrition Plus in the amount
  of $97,020.00 for the 2026 Summer Food Service Program; and, directed staff to take the

  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

11.  QUARTERLY CONTRACTS REPORT AS OF MARCH 31, 2026 – F2M25-40

  On August 26, 2024, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. O2M24-4837, implementing
  the California Uniform Public Construction Cost Accounting Act (CUPCCAA), as outlined
  in California Public Contract Code Sections 22000–22045. On April 28, 2025, the City
  Council adopted Ordinance No. O2M25-4845, updating contract thresholds in accordance
  with recent CUPCCAA amendments. During this meeting, the Council also requested a
  report identifying all contracts awarded between $50,000 and $75,000, which previously
  required Council approval before CUPCCAA implementation. During the reporting period
  of January 1, 2026 through March 31, 2026, there were eight contracts awarded in the
  amount of $50,000 to $75,000 without City Council approval.

  Discussion:  None

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the quarterly contracts report for the
  period of January 1, 2026 through March 31, 2026.

12.  NOTICE INVITING BIDS: SEWER MAIN REPLACEMENT PROJECT ON SEVENTH
  STREET BETWEEN VALLEY BOULEVARD AND SHORB STREET – F2M26-26,
  N2M26-50

  The City has been constructing the Alhambra Community Center at 612 W. Shorb Street.
  As part of this project, the sewer pipe was originally proposed to connect toward Seventh
  Street. However, because there was no City sewer main in front of the new building, the
  Utilities Department would be extending the main sewer line on Seventh Street and
  connecting it to the existing sewer main on Shorb Street. The existing sewer main on
  Shorb Street between Seventh Street and Sixth Street would be abandoned as part of this
  project. Plans and specifications were prepared. Staff reviewed the plans and found them
  to be consistent with the City’s standards.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the distribution of a Notice Inviting Bids to
  qualified contractors for the Sewer Main Replacement Project on Seventh Street between
  Valley Blvd. and Shorb St. with bids due no later than 10:30 a.m. on May 21, 2026 and

  8
4-27-26
   opened at 11:00 a.m. that same day; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary
  to finalize the Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

13.  RESOLUTION: FY 2026-2027 PROJECT IDENTIFICATION FOR THE ROAD REPAIR
  AND ACCOUNTABILITY ACT OF 2017 (SB1 BEALL) – F2M26-27, R2M26-11

  The Road Repair and Accountability Act stipulates that, prior to receiving Road
  Maintenance and Rehabilitation Account (RMRA) funds in a fiscal year, a city or county
  must submit to the California Transportation Commission (CTC) a project list pursuant to
  an adopted resolution. This information is due by July 1, 2026. Staff proposed a Street
  Rehabilitation Project for FY 2026-2027 that included design services and street
  rehabilitation (including but not limited to pavement, striping, ADA ramps, sidewalk, curb
  and gutter, etc.) on public streets bound by Atlantic Blvd., Garfield Ave., Huntington Dr.,
  Monterey Ave., Chapel Ave. and Main St. It was anticipated that the City would receive
  $2,318,224.00 from the RMRA Fund for FY 2026-2027.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M26-11 entitled: A
  Resolution of the City Council of the City of Alhambra, California adopting the Fiscal Year
  2026-27 list of projects funded by SB 1: The Road Repair and Accountability Act; and,
  directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

14.  AWARD CONTRACT: ALLEY REHABILITATION PROJECT (AREA B/PHASE I) –
  F2M26-20, N2M26-4, C2M26-24, M2M26-64

  On January 12, 2026 the City Council authorized a Notice Inviting Bids for distribution for
  the Alley Rehabilitation Project (Area B/Phase I) Project. On March 5, 2026, the City Clerk
  received 9 bids ranging from $282,381.00 (Estate Design and Construction, Inc.) to
  $617,250.00 (Van Engineering). Estate Design and Construction, Inc. submitted the
  lowest bid; however, it was deemed non-responsive for failing to provide the required
  documentation demonstrating experience with similar alley improvement projects. Staff
  further reviewed the bids and found the bid received from Towo Enterprises, Inc. in the
  amount of $395,925.00 to be the second lowest responsible bid. Towo Enterprises, Inc.
  had the necessary licenses to complete the work and had conducted similar scale projects
  in surrounding cities.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language approval
  by the City Manager and City Attorney, to Towo Enterprise, Inc., as the second lowest
  9
4-27-26
   responsive and responsible bidder in the amount of $395,925.00 for the Alley
  Rehabilitation Project Area B/Phase I; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary
  to finalize the Council’s action. (M2M26-64)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

15.  AWARD CONTRACT: ROOF REPLACEMENT AT CITY HALL (SOUTH STRUCTURE)
  – F2M26-26, N2M26-21, C2M26-25, M2M26-65

  A Notice Inviting Bids was approved for distribution by the City Council on February23,
  2026 for the Roof Replacement at City Hall (South Structure). The South Structure is the
  part of City Hall over the Parks and Recreation, Finance and City Clerks Departments. On
  April 9, 2026, the City Clerk received ten bids that ranged from $197,845.00 to
  $$529,115.00. Staff reviewed the bids and the Best Contracting Services bid in the amount
  of $197,845.00 is the lowest responsible bid. Best Contracting Services had the necessary
  licenses and was a certified installer for the selected roofing system. A reference check
  was conducted on similar projects completed, and it was satisfactory. This project was
  categorically exempt under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) in
  accordance with Title 14, Chapter 3, Section 15301, under Class 1.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language approval
  by the City Manager and the City Attorney, to Best Contracting Services, in the amount of
  $197,845.00 for the Roof Replacement at City Hall (South Structure); and, directed staff
  to undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s action. (M2M26-65)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

16.  AUTHORIZE RFP: TITLE VI PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT AND IMPLEMENTATION
  SERVICES – F2M26-29, RFP2M26-6

  As a recipient of Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) funds though Caltrans, the City
  must comply with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 requirements. The City was
  required to develop and implement a Title VI program subject to the review of Caltrans’
  Office of Local Civil Compliance. The project consisted of developing and implementing a
  Title VI Program as outlined by Caltrans’ Local Public Agency (LPA) requirements that
  mandate any agency receiving federal financial assistance not discriminate based on race,
  color, or national origin in any program or activity. Pursuant to the project, staff sought to
  distribute a Request for Proposals for the consultant services for Title VI Program
  Development and Implementation.

  Discussion:  None.

  10
4-27-26
   Action Taken:  City Council authorized the distribution of a Request for Proposals
  for Title VI Program Development Services, with proposals due no later than 4:00 p.m. on
  May 21, 2026.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

17.  ACCEPTANCE OF MEASURE A GRANT FUNDS FROM THE LOS ANGELES COUNTY
  REGIONAL PARK AND OPEN SPACE DISTRICT (RPOSD) FOR THE GREEN STREET
  DEMONSTRATION PROJECT AND THE FRONT STREET GREENWAY PROJECT –
  F2M26-18, M2M26-66

  The Los Angeles County Regional Park and Open Space District (RPOSD) protects over
  4,000 square miles of parks, beaches, and wildlife areas for residents and visitors. Marking
  a record investment, the latest round of Measure A grants provided over $78 million to

22.  FIRST READING OF AN ORDINANCE ADDING CHAPTER 6.29 (“RESIDENTIAL
  TENANT PROTECTIONS”) TO TITLE VI (HEALTH AND SANITATION) OF THE
  ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE ESTABLISHING AN INCREASED RELOCATION
  ASSISTANCE OBLIGATION ON CERTAIN NO-FAULT RESIDENTIAL EVICTIONS IN
  THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA – F2M26-7, O2M26-4861

  City Manager BINNQUIST provided a staff report. On April 13, 2026, the City Council
  directed staff to prepare an ordinance to increase relocation assistance payments for no-
  fault evictions from one (1) month to three (3) months’ rent. The proposed ordinance would
  add Chapter 6.29 to the City’s Municipal Code, requiring that in those circumstances
  where relocation assistance is required under AB 1482, that the obligation would be
  increased from one to three months. To the extent that an owner/landlord would not
  comply with this requirement, the ordinance provided that such noncompliance could be
  asserted as a defense in any action brought by the owner to recover possession of a
  residential unit. Under AB 1482, landlords would require to provide relocation assistance
  for certain no-fault evictions, including owner move-in, substantial rehabilitation,
  demolition, or withdrawal of units from the rental market.

  Public Comment:
  1) Jesus Rojas, representing the Apartment Association of Greater Los Angeles, also
  submitted comments to Council via a letter. He spoke against the proposed ordinance.

  2) David Bond, representing the Alhambra Tenant’s Union, discussed the state law AB
  1482 for tenant protections and the ways the ordinance was tied to it. He discussed the
  ways in which the proposed ordinance did not cover all tenants in Alhambra. He requested
  Council expand the scope of the proposed ordinance.

  3) Lewis McCammon suggested Council review the ability to expand the scope beyond
  state regulations. He further discussed the projects at 110 S. Chapel Ave. and 306 S.
  Cordova St., the eviction of tenants, and the loss of low-income housing in Alhambra. He
  requested clarification as to whether the proposed ordinance would apply to the tenants
  at 110 S. Chapel. He also suggested the City provide assistance through the Inclusionary
  Housing Trust Fund if the developer would not provide assistance to evicted tenants.

  Discussion:  Councilmember LEE discussed the application of AB1482 and the
  role of landlords as it would relate to 110 S. Chapel Ave. City Attorney MONTES provided
  clarification. Ms. LEE and Mr. MONTES continued to discuss the timing of the developer’s
  notice of eviction to tenants, the dates of property transfer, and the ability for the proposed
  13
4-27-26
   ordinance to apply to 110 S. Chapel Ave. after the fact. Ms. LEE went on to speak in
  support of the ordinance.

  Councilmember MAZA spoke in support of the ordinance and addressed concerns of
  “Mom and Pop” landlords and opponents to the ordinance.

  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER stated that she had heard of several other cases of no-
  fault evictions in the City. She supported the ordinance and discussed the hardship of
  renters and unaffordable housing conditions. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER motioned to
  approve the ordinance.

  Councilmember WANG discussed the need to support tenants and the concerns of “Mom
  and Pop” landlords. She spoke in support of the ordinance and the balance between
  providing assistance and the exception for smaller rental properties. Mr. MONTES
  provided clarification regarding type of ownership in AB 1482 and Management Analyst
  ALVAREZ provided further clarification regarding the type of rental unit. Mr. MAZA and
  Mr. MONTES discussed the obligation of the owner in cases of no cause, no fault eviction
  to provide notice of assistance.

  Mayor MALONEY discussed the implementation of Alhambra Housing Element, the City’s
  attempt to create more housing opportunities through high density areas and the
  unfortunate consequence in the case of 110 S. Chapel Ave. He stated that the intention
  of the proposed ordinance was to cover future cases such as 110 S. Chapel Ave. He
  requested staff continue to track similar cases going forward and added that this ordinance
  could not cover all cases at this time. He went on to address concerns of opponents to the
  ordinance and spoke in support of the ordinance. Mr. MALONEY seconded Ms. Andrade-
  Stadler’s motion to approve, and requested Council consider sending a letter to notify the
  developer at 110 S. Chapel Ave. of the ordinance and request they give the displaced
  tenants three months of rental assistance. He recognized that the City was not in a legal
  position to make this demand on the developer. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER accepted the
  amendment to her motion. Mr. MAZA clarified that the additional assistance would be two
  months’ rent in addition to the standard one month rent provided.

  Action Taken:  City Council agreed to send a letter to the current developer and
  property owner at 110 S. Chapel Ave informing them of the new ordinance and requesting
  additional rental assistance of 2 months’ rent be provided to displaced tenants; and
  declared introduced for its first reading the following ordinance entitled:

  Ordinance No. O2M26-4861: An Ordinance of the City Council of the City of
  Alhambra, California adding Chapter 6.29 (“Residential Tenant Protections”)
  to Title VI (Health and Sanitation) of the Alhambra Municipal Code establishing
  an increased relocation assistance obligation on certain no-fault residential
  evictions in the City of Alhambra

  which ordinance would return for a second reading and adoption at the next regular
  Council meeting.

 23.  NOVEMBER 3, 2026 ALHAMBRA GENERAL MUNICIPAL ELECTION: ADOPTION OF
  AN ORDINANCE CALLING THE ELECTION AND OF A RESOLUTION REGARDING
  CONSOLIDATION WITH THE STATEWIDE GENERAL ELECTION TO BE HELD THAT
  SAME DATE IN LOS ANGELES COUNTY – F2M26-33, O2M26-4859, R2M26-10

  On April 13, 2026, the City Council introduced for first reading Ordinance No. O2M26-
  4859 providing for a General Municipal Election to be held on November 3, 2026 for the
  purpose of submitting to the qualified voters the following named officers: Councilperson
  of the First District, full term; Councilperson of the Second District, full term; and,
  Councilperson of the Fifth District, full term. Pursuant to the Alhambra Charter as amended
  by Measure V in 2020, these offices shall be nominated from and elected by districts. The
  Alhambra City Charter provides that General Municipal Elections shall be consolidated
  with the Statewide General Elections to be held on the first Tuesday following the first
  Monday of every even-numbered year; hence, the next General Municipal Election for the
  City of Alhambra, will be held on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The City of Alhambra
  historically has consolidated its General Municipal Elections with those held on the same
  date in the County of Los Angeles. Based on economies of scale, such consolidation has
  resulted in considerable cost savings for the City. Therefore, staff requested that the City
  Council adopt the ordinance calling the November 3, 2026 General Municipal Election as
  well as a resolution regarding consolidation with the Statewide General Election to be held
  that same day in Los Angeles County.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council, by one motion, took the following actions:

  1.  Declared introduced for its second reading and adopt the following ordinance entitled:

  Ordinance No. O2M26-4859 entitled: An Ordinance of the Alhambra City
  Council providing for a General Municipal Election in said City to be held on
  November 3, 2026 and providing for the consolidation of the General Municipal
  Election with the Statewide General Election, said Election being held for the
  election of the following City Officials, to wit: Councilperson of the First District,
  full term; Councilperson of the Second District, full term; and, Councilperson
  of the Fifth District, full term; and,

  2.  Adopted Resolution No. R2M26-10 entitled: A Resolution of the Alhambra
  City Council requesting the Board of Supervisors of the County of Los Angeles
  to order the consolidation of an Alhambra General Municipal Election to be
  held on November 3, 2026 with the Statewide General Election to be held in
  Los Angeles County the same day, to authorize the Board of Supervisors of
  the County of Los Angeles to canvass the returns of said General Municipal
  Election and to request that the Registrar of Voters of said County be permitted
  to render specified services to the City of Alhambra relating to the conduct of
  said General Municipal Election pursuant to Elections Code Section 10403

  Staff requested that the City Council consider second reading and adoption of an
  ordinance approving a Zoning Text Amendment to amend Title 23 (Zoning) of the
  Alhambra Municipal Code to update Chapter 23.15 (Inclusionary Housing). Zoning Text
  Amendment AMD-26-03 is a City-initiated update to the City’s Inclusionary Housing
  Ordinance (IHO). The proposed updates were informed by implementation of the IHO over
  the past five years and are intended to improve clarity as well as align with state housing
  law-specifically, State Density Bonus Law. The proposed amendments maintain the City’s
  15% inclusionary unit requirement while revising affordability level requirements and
  simplifying compliance mechanisms. Updates to the Inclusionary Housing Regulations
  and Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fee schedule will ensure consistency with the proposed
  IHO updates. Adoption of these proposed updates aligns with the goals, policies, and
  objectives set forth in the City’s 2021-2029 Housing Element. The proposed ordinance
  was given first reading at the April 13, 2026 City Council meeting.

  Public Comment:  Lewis McCammon spoke in support of the proposed ordinance but
  noted the lack of provisions to encourage rental units as opposed to for-sale.
